claims.claim: Node handles many thousands of open sockets per process without trouble, and Go does too.
claims.measured: The I/O-wait test used only 256 connections: node-express 14,188 req/s, node-fastify 17,462 req/s, go-nethttp 18,905 req/s, go-gin 20,235 req/s
claims.why: The highest concurrency measured was 256 connections, so nothing shows how either runtime behaves with thousands of open sockets.

claims.claim: At this scale (up to 2,500 deliveries/s, mostly waiting) either language runs on a few small machines.
claims.about: Node.js vs Go for I/O-bound work
claims.measured: I/O wait (10 ms per request) on 1 CPU: node-fastify 17,462 req/s at 76% CPU, node-express 14,188 req/s at 92% CPU, go-gin 20,235 req/s at 47% CPU, go-nethttp 18,905 req/s at 57% CPU
claims.why: Both stacks handled well over 2,500 I/O-bound requests/s on a single CPU, so a few small machines is a safe figure (though the benchmark served requests rather than making slow outbound calls).

claims.claim: The cloud bill difference between Node and Go is maybe tens of dollars a month.
claims.why: The measurements contain no cost figures, and they don't cover the outbound-call workload this estimate depends on.

claims.claim: Go suits the job well, with cheap concurrency and low memory.
claims.measured: I/O wait peak memory: go-gin 16 MB, go-nethttp 15 MB vs node-express 68 MB, node-fastify 69 MB; Go reached 18,905–20,235 req/s at 47–57% CPU vs Node's 14,188–17,462 req/s at 76–92% CPU
claims.why: Go used about 4x less memory and less CPU than Node for more I/O-bound throughput, which supports the claim.
